claims.text: The selected high-entropy alloy has a random atomic configuration.
The superconducting behavior of the initial alloy is uncharacterized.
Controlled thermal annealing can systematically vary the alloy's degree of atomic disorder.
Compositional tuning can systematically vary the alloy's degree of atomic disorder.
Controlled atomic disorder induces local lattice distortions.
Moderate atomic disorder increases local lattice distortions.
The disorder-induced local lattice distortions enhance electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling facilitates Cooper-pair formation.
Cooper-pair formation leads to superconductivity at low temperature.
Excessive disorder may fail to provide conditions favorable for superconductivity.
Insufficient disorder may fail to provide conditions favorable for superconductivity.
An optimal moderate level of atomic disorder will produce a measurable superconducting transition relative to the as-synthesized baseline.
The predicted superconducting transition will be evidenced by both a drop in electrical resistivity and a diamagnetic response.
The initial alloy does not exhibit superconductivity or exhibits only very weak superconducting properties.
The proposed mechanism should hold for single-phase high-entropy alloys with similar mixing entropy.
The proposed mechanism may not hold for alloys with significantly different compositions, extreme disorder, or multiphase structures.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as having uncharacterized superconducting behavior, but the baseline presumes that it has no superconductivity or only very weak superconductivity.
The experiment calls for samples with identical compositions while also proposing compositional tuning as a means of varying disorder; compositional tuning cannot preserve identical composition.
